### page_1
Paleomagnetism of Middle Proterozoic mafic intrusions and
Upper Proterozoic (Nankoweap) red beds from the
Lower Grand Canyon Supergroup, Arizona
Arlo B. Weil a,*, John W. Geissman b, Matt Heizler c, Rob V an der V ood
a Department of Geology, Bryn Mawr College, 101 Merion Avenue, Bryn Mawr , P A 19010-2899, USA
b Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM 87131, USA
c New Mexico Bureau of Mines and Mineral Resources, New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, NM 87801, USA
d Department of Geologic Sciences, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor , MI 48109, USA
Received 3 April 2002; received in revised form 12 November 2002; accepted 5 June 2003
Abstract
Paleomagnetic data from lavas and dikes of the Unkar igneous suite (16 sites) and sedimentary rocks of the Nankoweap
Formation (7 sites), Grand Canyon Supergroup (GCSG), Arizona, provide two primary paleomagnetic poles for Laurentia for the
latest Middle Proterozoic (ca. 1090 Ma) at 32 jN, 185jE (dp = 6.8j, dm = 9.3j) and early Late Proterozoic (ca. 850 – 900 Ma) at
10jS, 163jE (dp = 3.5j, dm = 7.0j). A new
40Ar/39Ar age determination from an Unkar dike gives an interpreted intrusion age of
about 1090 Ma, similar to previously reported geochronologic data for the Cardenas Basalts and associated intrusions. The
paleomagnetic data show no evidence of any younger, middle Late Proterozoic tectonothermal event such as has been revealed in
previous geochronologic studies of the Unkar igneous suite. The pole position for the Unkar Group Cardenas Basalts and related
intrusions is in good agreement with other ca. 1100 Ma paleomagnetic poles from the Keweenawan midcontinent rift deposits and
other SW Laurentia diabase intrusions. The close agreement in age and position of the Unkar intrusion (UI) pole with poles derived
from rift related rocks from elsewhere in Laurentia indicates that mafic magmatism was essentially synchronous and widespread
throughout Laurentia at ca. 1100 Ma, suggesting a large-scale continental magmatic event. The pole position for the Nankoweap
Formation, which plots south of the Unkar mafic rocks, is consistent with a younger age of deposition, at about 900 to 850 Ma, than
had previously been proposed. Consequently, the inferred f 200 Ma difference in age between the Cardenas Basalts and
overlying Nankoweap Formation provides evidence for a third major unconformity within the Grand Canyon sequence.
D 2003 Elsevier B.V . All rights reserved.
Keywords: Rodinia; Proterozoic paleogeography; Paleomagnetism; Grand Canyon Supergroup; Continental magmatism
1. Introduction
With the increasing popularity of research focused
on the proposed Rodinia supercontinent and its sub-
sequent dispersal (Hoffman, 1991; Dalziel, 1992,
1997; Weil et al., 1998; Meert and Powell, 2001;
Hartz and Torsvik, 2002) , it is crucial to acquire more
robust, well-dated paleomagnetic datasets from Pre-
cambrian cratons that allow for the creation of more
accurately defined paleogeographic reconstructions
for the Middle and Late Proterozoic. Reliable paleo-

doi:10.1016/S0040-1951(03)00339-1
* Corresponding author. Fax: +1-610-5265086.

Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199 – 220

### page_2
magnetic data from Precambrian sedimentary and
igneous rocks are vital for reconstructing the tectonic
and paleogeographic evolution of the Rodinia super-
continent. Tests of Proterozoic plate reconstructions
rely heavily on properly demagnetized rocks that yield
well-dated primary paleomagnetic poles, of which
there are very few (Buchan et al., 2000) . Currently,
there are far too many gaps in the paleomagnetic
record of most Rodinia cratons to make robust esti-
mates of apparent polar wander path (APWP) seg-
ments and, thus, predictions on the details of the
relative position of individual cratons and, in partic-
ular, on global paleogeography (Powell et al., 1993) .
The cratons for which reliable data exist typically
have incomplete APWPs and/or many individual
paleomagnetic results that lack reliable absolute age
assignment. To improve on the paleomagnetic data-
base for the Proterozoic of Laurentia, a comprehen-
sive sampling effort has been done throughout the
Grand Canyon Supergroup (GCSG), Arizona (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. Simplified geologic map of Precambrian rocks exposed in the Grand Canyon, Arizona. Modified from Timmons et al. (2001) .
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220200

### page_3
This study reports new paleomagnetic results from
Middle Proterozoic igneous rocks of the lower GCSG
and the Upper Proterozoic Nankoweap Formation.
The GCSG is one of the thickest, best preserved
and regionally unmetamorphosed Proterozoic sequen-
ces in the US for much of the time during which the
Rodinia supercontinent existed (1300 – 750 Ma). The
entire GCSG lies unconformably on top of crystalline
basement of the Vishnu Schist. The Vishnu Schist was
formed during ca. 1.7 Ga metamorphism (Hawkins
and Bowring, 1999) and cooled below f 200 jC
between 1200 and 1300 Ma (Karlstrom et al., 1997;
Timmons et al., 2001) . A volcanic ash layer in the
Bass limestone near the base of the GCSG is dated at
1253 F 3 Ma (S. Bowring, unpublished data) giving a
basal age of f 1300 Ma. The GCSG is capped
unconformably by the Middle Cambrian Tapeats
sandstone of the Tonto Group (Fig. 2) . The GCSG
is divided into two major groups: the Unkar Group
(lower GCSG) and the Chuar Group (upper GCSG).
The lower GCSG was deposited between 1300 (Bass
Limestone) and 1100 Ma (Cardenas Basalts), whereas
the upper GCSG was deposited beginning at about
800 Ma during initial Rodinia breakup and Cordillera
margin formation (Karlstrom et al., 2000) .S a n d -
wiched between the lower and upper GCSG groups
is the enigmatic Nankoweap Formation, a thin red bed
sequence whose absolute age is yet to be determined
(Fig. 2) .
The lower GCSG is composed of red sandstones,
siltstones and shales, as well as limestone and dolo-
mite layers, and is capped by a 300-m-thick extrusive
sequence—the Cardenas Basalts. Cross-cutting lower
GCSG strata are numerous mafic intrusions that are
proposed to be feeders for the Cardenas Basalts. The
most recent isotopic age determinations for the lavas
yield a Rb – Sr whole-rock age of 1103 F 66 Ma
(Larson et al., 1994) . The petrographic and geochem-
ical relationship between the Cardenas Basalts and
mafic dikes has been studied by Hendricks (1989) and
Larson et al. (1994) , who concluded that the lavas and
intrusions were derived from a similar magma source.
Initial paleomagnetic studies of these rocks (Elston
and Scott, 1973) were promising in that the preserved
magnetizations, albeit on the basis of limited demag-
netization work, did not resemble those typical of
most of the Phanerozoic, suggesting that they had not
been remagnetized during younger geologic events.
A paleomagnetic, rock magnetic and
40Ar/39Ar
geochronologic investigation of the mafic igneous
rocks within the lower GCSG and the overlying
Nankoweap Formation was undertaken to better un-
derstand the extent, timing and tectonic significance
of large-scale extension within the Rodinia Supercon-
tinent at f 1100 Ma, and to better define Laurentia’s
late Middle and early Late Proterozoic APWP .
Fig. 2. Simplified stratigraphic section of the Grand Canyon
Supergroup, Arizona. Age estimates are provided at the right of the
column and are discussed in the text. Column modified from Dehler
et al. (2001) .
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220 201

### page_4
2. Geologic setting
The GCSG, Arizona, records two episodes of latest
Middle and Late Proterozoic extension along the
ancient Cordilleran margin of Laurentia. The first
event, broadly synchronous with Grenville tectonism
to the east and southeast (Link et al., 1993; Timmons
et al., 2001) , is ca. 1250 – 1100 Ma, and is represented
by deposition of Unkar Group strata. The second
event, approximately synchronous with rifting of the
Rodinia supercontinent, is ca. 800 – 740 Ma, and is
represented by sedimentary rocks of the Chuar Group
(Karlstrom et al., 2000) . These two major groups are
separated by the Nankoweap Formation, which is
bound at its top and bottom by slight angular uncon-
formities (Elston and Scott, 1976) .H o w e v e r ,t h e
duration and importance of the Nankoweap uncon-
formities and, thus, the time interval missing between
the two Proterozoic extensional events, is still poorly
understood (Elston, 1993; Lucchitta and Hendricks,
1983; Timmons et al., 2001) .
The Unkar Group is interpreted as a shallow
marine to locally subaerial sequence of lagoonal, tidal
flat and deltaic sediments (Hendricks and Stevenson,
1990; Elston, 1989a,b; Link et al., 1993) . Deposition
of the Unkar Group appears to be discontinuous. The
1253-Ma volcanic ash indicates the Bass Limestone to
be about this age. However,
40Ar/39Ar dating of
detrital muscovite from the basal, Escalante Creek
Member of the Dox Sandstone indicates the Dox
Sandstone is younger than 1140 Ma (Heizler et al.,
1999), but older than the 1103 F 66 Ma capping
Cardenas Basalts. Timmons et al. (2001) attempted
to better define the age of the Cardenas Basalts and
associated intrusions using the
40Ar/39Ar step-heating
method. Although the age spectra are disturbed and
yield total gas age estimates ranging from about 988
to about 771 Ma, they conclude that the lavas and
dikes were emplaced by at least 1050 Ma, consistent
with the Rb/Sr data reported by Elston and McKee
(1982) and Larson et al. (1994) . The disturbance in
Cardenas age spectra reported by Timmons et al.
(2001) was presumably related to a younger alteration
and/or low-temperature heating event (Larson et al.,
1994).
The Unkar Group is exposed in full and half
grabens within the canyon (Sears, 1990) . Field evi-
dence for deposition in an extensional setting
includes: dramatic thickness changes in sedimentary
units across faults with Proterozoic ancestry, soft
sediment deformation, an angular unconformity with
the overlying Nankoweap Formation and intraforma-
tional faults (Sears, 1990; Timmons et al., 2001) . The
overall structural features documenting extension
within the Unkar Group show a southwest-directed
extension direction similar to other proposed Lauren-
tia extensional settings at ca. 1100 Ma (Karlstrom and
Humphreys, 1998) . The most notable features sup-
porting extension during this time are the mid-conti-
nent and Keweenawan rift systems of eastern North
America, the Mojave and Arizona terranes and the
Apache and Pahrump groups of southwest North
America. The geologic setting and available geochro-
nologic data for these regions indicate that mafic
magmatism is temporally correlative and was largely
confined to the period ca. 1070 – 1100 Ma (see Harlan,
1993 for a review of available age dates). The cause of
this broad tectonomagmatic event affecting much of
Laurentia is still debated. Some of the explanations
include: (1) Grenville deformation that caused NE –
SW extension (Lambeck, 1983; DeRito et al., 1983) ,
(2) intracratonic rifting, (3) mantle insulation (Hoff-
man, 1989) and (4) southwest North American crust
under tectonic compression or an isotropic state of
stress at 1.1 Ga (Howard, 1991) .
The Cardenas Basalts cap the Unkar Group and
were first studied by Powell (1876) and Waltcott
(1883). This 300-m-thick sequence of tholeiitic ba-
salt has been subdivided into a lower 100-m-thick
coarse-grained, ophitic olivine tholeiite and an upper
200-m-thick fine grained, aphyric quartz tholeiite and
tholeiitic andesite (Hendricks, 1989; Larson et al.,
1994). Both sequences were erupted subaerially
(Larson et al., 1994) , with some evidence of sub-
aqueous eruptions in the lower unit (Elston and
Mckee, 1982; Lucchitta and Hendricks, 1983) . There
are at least 12 mappable flows preserved, but it is
unclear how many flows existed in the past as the
upper surface of the Cardenas Basalts is truncated by
Proterozoic erosion (Larson et al., 1994) . Beds of
siltstone and sandstone are distributed throughout the
Cardenas Basalts (Lucchitta and Hendricks, 1983) ,
suggesting periods of quiescence between eruptive
flows. Geochemical and isotopic data from the
Cardenas Basalts and associated intrusions cutting
Unkar strata indicate a genetic relationship between
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220202

### page_5
these igneous rocks, from a slightly enriched peri-
dotitic mantle source (Hendricks, 1989; Larson et al.,
1994). However, no feeder relationships have ever
been found that can directly link intrusive and
extrusive rocks (Hendricks, 1989) . Postemplace-
ment/cooling temperatures of the igneous suite never
exceeded temperatures of 250 jC and pressures of
1.5 kbar (Larson et al., 1994) .
The Nankoweap Formation is a 113 – 250-m-thick
sequence consisting entirely of hematite-cemented
sandstones (Elston and Scott, 1976) . The Nankoweap
Formation was first identified and described by Va n
Gundy (1934, 1951) , but was not formally classified
and isolated as a formation until the mapping of
Maxson (1961) . This red bed sequence is unconform-
ably bound below by the Unkar Group and above by
the Chuar Group. The exact genetic relationship of the
Nankoweap to older and younger GCSG strata
remains poorly understood (Timmons et al., 2001) .
Furthermore, the age of the formation is undeter-
mined, and has been proposed to be anywhere from
1100 Ma (Elston and Scott, 1976; Elston, 1989b) and,
thus, just slightly younger than the Unkar Group, to as
young as about f 900 Ma (Lucchitta and Hendricks,
1983) and, thus, closer to the age of inception of
deposition of the Chuar Group. Elston and Scott
(1976) proposed that the Nankoweap Formation
should be divided into two distinct members, a lower
ferruginous member and an upper member. Support
for this subdivision was based on preliminary paleo-
magnetic data from the proposed lower ferruginous
member (Elston, 1989a,c) that were interpreted to be
similar to preliminary results from the Cardenas
Basalts (Elston and Scott, 1973) . Moreover, Elston
(1989c) argued that the redbeds from the lower
member of the Nankoweap Formation have strong
lithologic similarities to red beds within the underly-
ing Cardenas Basalts sequence. Lucchitta and Hen-
dricks (1983) argued that the lower ferruginous
Nankoweap member is in fact part of the underlying
Unkar Group, specifically part of the underlying
Cardenas Basalts, and that the upper Nankoweap
member records much younger deposition. Field ev-
idence suggests that the entire Nankoweap section
was deposited in an active extensional environment as
evidenced by intraformational faults and soft-sedi-
ment deformation (Elston and Scott, 1973; Elston,
1993; Timmons et al., 2001) .
The overlying Chuar Group is composed of about
1700 m of sedimentary rock, and is interpreted as
dominantly shallow marine and tidal flat deposits,
with intermittent deeper water facies (Dehler et al.,
2001). Shale, siltstone, sandstone, limestone and do-
lomite dominate the Chuar rock types in contrast to
the generally red sandstone-dominated Unkar Group
sequence. A U – Pb date of 742 F 6 Ma on an ash
layer was reported for the upper part of the Chuar
Group by Karlstrom et al. (2000) . Field evidence for
regional extension during the Chuar Group deposition
includes intraformational faults, large-scale asymmet-
ric synclines that tighten with depth, suggesting syn-
chronous folding and deposition (Timmons et al.,
2001), and the genetic relationship between synclines
(i.e., Chuar syncline) and faults with Proterozoic
ancestry (e.g., Butte fault) (Elston and Mckee,
1982). In contrast to the NW structural grain found
in the Unkar Group, the Chuar Group is characterized
by a NS structural grain. The extensional phase
recorded by the Chuar Group is thought to be a
manifestation of the Neoproterozoic breakup of Rodi-
nia ( Dehler et al., 2001 ; Karlstrom et al., 2000;
Timmons et al., 2001 ).
3. Sampling and experimental methods
Some 250 hand samples were collected in the fall
of 1998 and 1999 at 18 sites from the Unkar mafic
igneous suite, 6 sites from host Unkar sediments and
8 sites from the Nankoweap Formation (Fig. 3) . Site
locations were distributed along the main Grand
Canyon corridor; severely weathered and highly
faulted areas were avoided where possible. Oriented
hand samples were collected in the field using a
geologic hammer, chisel and magnetic compass (col-
lection of samples using a portable field drill is no
longer allowed in the Grand Canyon). Bedding ori-
entations were measured in the field using a magnetic
compass.
Seven to ten standard 2.54-cm-diameter paleomag-
netic specimens (one per independently oriented sam-
ple) from each site were progressively demagnetized
in a thermal demagnetizer and measured in a three-
axes cryogenic magnetometer in the field-free room at
the University of Michigan’s paleomagnetic laborato-
ry. Heating was carried out in 50 jC increments to a
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220 203

### page_6
maximum temperature of 680 jC, with reduced incre-
ments at temperatures above 350 jC. Alternating field
(AF) demagnetization was performed with a Sapphire
Instruments SI-4 AF demagnetizer. However, the AF
treatment did not adequately and/or fully isolate the
principal components of remanence due to the pres-
ence of higher coercivity mineral phases (see rock
magnetism section). In the thermally treated samples,
remanence directions were calculated from principal
component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) of linear de-
magnetization trajectories identified on paleomagnetic
orthogonal projection plots (Zijderveld, 1967) . Site-
mean directions were calculated by averaging the
sample directions, using the method of Fisher (1953) .
Where possible, baked contact tests (Everitt and
Clegg, 1962) were performed to define the relative
age of magnetization acquisition for the mafic intru-
sions and fold tests were performed to characterize the
Fig. 3. Geologic map of the main Colorado River corridor through the Grand Canyon, Arizona. Sample site locations highlighted by filled and
open symbols. Open circles: Unkar Group intrusions. Grey circles: Unkar Group intrusion contact rock. Grey triangles: Cardenas Basalts. Open
stars: Nankoweap Formation. Map modified from Huntoon et al. (1996) .
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220204

### page_7
relative age of magnetization acquisition by the Nan-
koweap sediments. At localities where field tests
could not be done, comparison of characteristic mag-
netization directions with field-tested sites was made
to attempt to assess the relative timing of magnetiza-
tion acquisition.
Hysteresis properties of core specimens were mea-
sured with a Princeton Vibrating Sample Magnetome-
ter (Micro VSM). Isothermal remanent magnetizations
(IRM) were imparted with an electromagnet in fields up
to 1.2 T. Finally, thermal demagnetization of three-axes
IRM (Lowrie, 1990) was performed on representative
samples at the University of New Mexico. For the
three-axes measurements, an IRM was first imparted
down the long axis of the cores ( z-axis) with the
maximum available field of 3.0 T. Subsequently, 0.3
and 0.03 T fields were applied along the y and x-axes,
respectively.
Two mafic sills (H98-131.6-2, GC9825) collected
at river miles 131.6 (Gallaway Canyon) and 109.5
(near the Bass Trail), respectively, were dated by the
40Ar/39Ar method. Biotite from H98-131.6-2 was
collected from the contact between the sill and the
sediments and is interpreted to have grown during sill
emplacement. Biotite occurs as a primary phase in
GC9825 and was separated directly from the sill. The
biotite samples were irradiated at the University of
Michigan Ford Reactor in the L67 position for 100
h along with Fish Canyon Sanidine with an assigned
age of 27.84 Ma. Following irradiation, the samples
were step-heated in a double vacuum Mo resistance
furnace and extracted argon was analyzed within an
MAP-215-50 mass spectrometer.
4. Results
4.1. Rock magnetism
Several rock magnetic approaches were taken to
better understand the overall magnetic mineralogy of
the rocks investigated. The documentation of these
results, in the context of demonstrating the likelihood
that the rocks studied carry ancient and in most cases
primary or near-primary magnetizations, is an impor-
tant facet of our research. IRM measurements were
made on core specimens from 15 samples from Unkar
Group igneous rocks (Fig. 4) . In 12 of the 15 speci-
mens measured, IRM was acquired rapidly in low
fields (less than 0.2 T), becoming completely saturat-
ed by 0.3 T, indicating a dominance of low- to
medium-coercivity mineral phases such as magnetite
or titanomagnetite (Fig. 4a) . In the remaining three
samples of much lower IRM intensities, a higher
coercivity mineral phase was present that could not
be saturated with the available fields (Fig. 4b) . He-
matite is the likely candidate for this higher coercivity
phase.
Hysteresis measurements were made on 18 core
specimens. Several examples of hysteresis loops re-
veal saturation by 1.0 T and exhibit typical pseudo-
Fig. 4. Typical isothermal remanent magnetization acquisition
curves for samples of the Unkar igneous rocks containing (a) only
low-coercivity mineral phases and (b) both low- and high-coercivity
mineral phases.
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220 205

### page_8
single-domain (PSD), magnetite-dominated uncon-
stricted loops (Fig. 5a and b) . Ratios of saturation
remanence (Mr) to saturation magnetization (Ms) for
those specimens that saturate range from 0.09 to 0.48
(Fig. 5c) . Ratios of coercivity of remanence (Hcr) to
coercivity (Hc) range from 1.4 to 2.9 (Fig. 5c) . With
respect to domain state distributions on a Day plot
(Day et al., 1977) , Mr/Ms and Hcr/Hc values for
saturated samples lie in the PSD field for magnetite.
The three samples that displayed a higher coercivity
phase in IRM acquisition experiments were charac-
terized by unsaturated wasp-waisted hysteresis loops.
Furthermore, the wasp-waisted geometry of the loops
(Fig. 5d) indicates a bimodal distribution of magnetic
phases, likely the combination of low- to medium-
coercivity magnetite and higher coercivity hematite.
The presence of hematite as a remanence carrier is
supported by high laboratory unblocking temperatures
(up to 680 jC) for many of the Unkar igneous rocks
(Figs. 6 and 7) . Demagnetization response, described
below, shows the contribution of both magnetite and
hematite to the total NRM of most samples (Fig. 6a) .
To further test the magnetic mineralogy of the
igneous samples, thermal demagnetization of three-
axes IRM (Lowrie, 1990) (Fig. 8) allows magnetic
minerals with contrasting coercivities to be identified
Fig. 5. (a and b) Typical examples of hysteresis loops from Unkar intrusions showing saturation by 1.0 T and typical pseudo-single-domain
(PSD), magnetite-dominated unconstricted loops. (c) Hysteresis ratios plotted according to Day et al. (1977) for Unkar intrusions. Filled
diamonds distinguishes the samples that were characterized by saturated hysteresis loops (low-coercivity magnetite), and open circles
distinguished the samples that had unsaturated wasp-waisted hysteresis loops (combination of low-coercivity magnetite and high-coercivity
hematite). (d) Example of a hysteresis loop from Unkar intrusions showing an unsaturated wasp-waisted hysteresis loop typical for mixtures of
low-coercivity magnetite and high-coercivity hematite.
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220206

### page_9
according to their respective unblocking temperatures.
Five representative samples were analyzed. The IRM
intensities of these samples, even along the z compo-
nent (3.0 T applied field), are all above 100 A/m, and
in several cases at least an order of magnitude higher.
The dominant magnetic mineral present is activated in
0.3 T and the IRM acquired is largely unblocked
below about 580 jC (Fig. 8) . We interpret the phase
that unblocks below about 580 jC to be nearly pure
magnetite. Some samples (in particular J4M, AW14F,
and Card22B) show evidence of the discrete unblock-
ing of a second phase at temperatures near or below
400 jC. This phenomenon may be caused by a
mixture of coarse maghemite and/or pyrrhotite. Above
about 600 jC, the magnetization along the x compo-
nent is essentially zero, while that along the y and in
particular z component smoothly unblocks up to about
675 jC, indicating the relative abundance of hematite.
Together, hysteresis measurements, IRM acquisition
curves, unblocking temperatures of NRM and three-
axes IRM indicate that low-titanium magnetite is the
dominant magnetization carrier in Unkar igneous
rocks with a measurable contribution from the higher
coercivity mineral hematite.
4.2. Paleomagnetism
4.2.1. Unkar igneous rocks
Demagnetization behavior of most Unkar intru-
sions is relatively straightforward. NRM intensities
ranged from 40 to 2500 mA/m. Typical demagnetiza-
tion response shows that most samples carry a uni-
vectorial ancient magnetization component with a
minor secondary component (Fig. 7) . The secondary
component, in geographic coordinates, has a north-
seeking declination and a moderate positive inclina-

intrusives. Filled (open) symbols indicate projections onto the horizontal (vertical) plane. (c) Three typical demagnetization plots of
representative samples from site aw25 collected along the contract of the Lizard Dike. (d) Three typical demagnetization plots of representative
samples from Dox Formation collected at a distance of at least three dike-widths from any observed intrusion.
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220208

### page_11
tion, which is subparallel to the Earth’s present-day
field (PDF) at the sampling location. The PDF com-
ponent is likely a viscous overprint and is usually
removed by 250 jC, with a few exceptions that are
not removed until 350 jC.
After removal of the viscous secondary PDF com-
ponent, most Unkar igneous rocks yield a single
component of magnetization that exhibits linear decay
to the origin of a demagnetization diagram, which we
infer to be the rock’s ancient characteristic remanence
Fig. 8. Thermal demagnetization intensity versus temperature plots of three-component IRM, acquired along the specimen z-axis (3.0 T), y-axis
(0.3 T) and x-axis (0.03 T), following the method of Lowrie (1990) .
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220 209

### page_12
direction (ChRM). This ChRM has a west to west –
northwest-seeking declination and a moderate positive
inclination (Fig. 7a and b) (Table 1) .
All Cardenas Basalt sites were collected from
individual flows. Of the five sites collected, only three
sites gave interpretable results. The remaining two
sites (J3 and Card21) had a combination of unresolv-
able ChRM directions and/or ChRM directions that
were highly dispersed and therefore did not yield an
acceptable site mean direction. A likely explanation
for the irregular behavior of the two sites is alteration
due to geologically recent subaerial weathering. Sites
J3 and Card21 were the most ferruginous and visibly
altered of the sites collected. The three sites that
responded well to demagnetization yielded a univec-
torial ChRM component of west-seeking declination
and a moderate positive inclination. In all cases, the
ChRM was isolated between 250 and 680 jC. De-
magnetization directions were well defined for indi-
vidual specimens with maximum angular deviation
(MAD) values less than 10 j.
The Unkar intrusions sampled range in (exposed)
geometry from simple dikes, with widths typically
less than 5 m, to more irregular, small dome-shaped
features with maximum dimensions measured in tens
of meters. All 13 sites from Unkar intrusions gave
interpretable results. The ChRM was isolated between
300 and 580 jC with many samples carrying this
remanence up to 680 jC. In all cases, the ChRM is of
west-seeking declination and a moderate positive
inclination (Fig. 7) . The fact that both magnetite and
hematite contribute as carriers of the ancient rema-
nence in the Unkar intrusions and Cardenas Basalts is
interpreted to indicate that the rocks have a primary
TRM, residing in low titanium magnetite, and an early
acquired chemical magnetization in hematite and
possibly maghemite, likely acquired during oxidation
of the lava in cooling to ambient temperatures. Oxi-

dation could have been stimulated by interaction of
the igneous rock, at subsolidus conditions, with either
a body of water (as has been proposed for parts of the
Cardenas Basalts; Elston and Mckee, 1982; Lucchitta
and Hendricks, 1983 ) or with water-saturated sedi-
ment (in this case, the Dox Formation). Interestingly,
all sites in intrusive rocks collected from the lower
parts of the Unkar Group (possibly intruded into more
lithified sediment as opposed to water saturated un-
consolidated sediment) had magnetizations with lab-
oratory unblocking temperatures below 580 jC. The
ChRM directions from those sites in which magnetite
Fig. 10. Typical demagnetization plots of representative samples from the Nankoweap Formation, GCSG, in geographic coordinates. Filled
(open) symbols indicate projections onto the horizontal (vertical) plane.

### page_14
is the principal remanence carrier and those sites in
which both magnetite and hematite carry the ancient
remanence are statistically indistinguishable (Table 1)
and, thus, are not separated for directional analysis.
Several sites were collected for the purpose of
performing baked contact tests between Unkar Group
strata and the dikes and lavas. One site was collected
from the Hakatai Shale (aw33), and five sites were
collected from the host Dox Sandstone conformably
underlying Cardenas Basalts. Sites aw25 and aw34
were collected along the contact of the Lizard Dike
system, sites aw28 and aw35 were collected at least
several dike-widths away from the Lizard Dike intru-
sions, and site aw15 was collected near the Tanner
rapid dikes (Fig. 3) . Typical demagnetization dia-
grams are shown in Fig. 7c , and paleomagnetic site
information is given in Table 1. At site aw25, samples
were collected at incremental distances away from the
main Lizard dike. At the dike contact, the Dox
samples have the highest magnetization intensities
(14.9 mA/m) and the ChRM shows a linear decay to
the origin of the demagnetization plot (Fig. 7c) with
the ChRM being isolated between 200 and 680 jC
(Fig. 6b) . At 10 cm away from the dike contact,
perpendicular to the strike of the dike, the magneti-
zation is slightly weaker (9.9 mA/m) and is isolated
between 250 and 680 jC. At a half-dike width away
from the contact, the intensity drops even lower (2.2
mA/m) and the ChRM is isolated between 600 and
680 jC (Fig. 7c) . A similar pattern characterized the
response from sites aw33 and aw34. Site aw35,
collected from the Hakatai Shale, did not give inter-
pretable results. The remaining two sites in Dox strata
were collected several dike-widths away from any
observed intrusions and were characterized by unsta-
ble demagnetization behavior and/or random direc-
tions (Fig. 7d) . However, two specimens from Dox
Formation strata at site aw28 had no obvious spatial
association with any intrusions yet carry a ChRM that
is well-defined in progressive demagnetization and
that is west-seeking and moderately down (Fig. 7d) .
These specimens likely reflect a primary magnetiza-
tion that is slightly older than that of the intrusions.
The ensemble of results from the contact tests provide
a partially positive baked contact result that indicates
that the intrusion of the dikes resulted in a secondary
thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) in immediately
adjacent host Dox Sandstone strata that is subparallel
to the ChRM acquired by cross-cutting dikes during
initial cooling after emplacement.
Because of the similarity in site-mean directions
between the extrusive and intrusive rocks (Fig. 9), the
two groups were combined for the purposes of pro-
viding a grand mean paleomagnetic direction. After
structural corrections for tilt ( Fig. 9; Table 1), the total
of 16 accepted sites from the Unkar igneous suite
gives a mean paleomagnetic direction of D = 285.5j,
I =57.0j (k = 33.9, a
95 = 6.4j, n = 16) (Fig. 9) .
4.2.2. Nankoweap Formation
NRM intensities for Nankoweap Formation red
beds range from 2.1 to 32.2 mA/m. Typical demag-
netization response shows that almost all samples
carry a single univectorial magnetization component
with a minor secondary component. The secondary
component in in situ coordinates has a north-seeking
declination and a moderate positive inclination, which
is subparallel to the Earth’s present-day field (PDF) at
the sampling location. The PDF component is re-
moved by 200 jC and is likely a viscous overprint.
After removal of the viscous PDF component,
most Nankoweap Formation specimens yield a single
magnetization component that exhibits linear decay to
the origin of a demagnetization diagram, which we
interpret to be the ancient ChRM of these rocks. This
ChRM has a west –southwest declination with a
shallow inclination ( Fig. 10, Table 2). Several samples

Seven of the eight Nankoweap sites provide
interpretable results based on stable demagnetization
behavior and well-grouped magnetizations. Demag-
netization directions were well-defined for individual
specimens. Any specimen with a MAD value greater
than 10 j was not used for directional analysis. The
ChRM was isolated between 300 and 680 jC. The
rejected site (nanko-28), is located immediately be-
neath the unconformity between lowermost Chuar
Group strata and the Nankoweap Formation. During
thermal demagnetization, rocks from this site exhibit
unstable, spurious behavior above 300 jC; the
results were discarded from further analysis.

(Fig. 3) , bedding orientations in these strata range
in dip direction from northeast to southwest, afford-

reach a peak clustering at about 80% unfolding,
with a kappa value of 95 (McElhinny, 1964) .T o

parametric bootstrap fold test was applied (Tauxe,
1998), which gives a similar result of maximum
clustering at f 80% unfolding and a 95% confi-
dence interval that includes 100% unfolding (Fig.
11a). Given that the Chuar Group unconformably
(angular) overlies the Nankoweap Formation and
field evidence supports deposition of Nankoweap
strata concurrent with deformation, the fold test is
interpreted to indicate a prefolding, and very early
acquired (primary) magnetization for the Nanko-

the combined seven sites from the Nankoweap

4.3. 40Ar/ 39Ar age determination
The two biotite age spectra ( Fig. 12 , Table 3) are,
overall, interpretable although of mixed behavior.
Sample H98-131.6-2 yields a generally flat age spec-
trum with a weighted mean age of 1090.6 F 4.5 Ma
(Fig. 12 ; Table 3 ). The steps used for the weighted
mean have a slightly elevated mean square weighted
deviation (MSWD) value of 2.83 that falls above the
95% confidence level predicted for 5 degrees of
freedom (cf. Mahon, 1996 ). Therefore, the calculated
weighted mean uncertainty (Taylor, 1982) has been
multiplied by the square root of the MSWD. The
1090.6 F 4.5 Ma age is interpreted as the intrusion
age of this sill ( F 2r error). Biotite from 98GC-25
yields a more complex age spectrum (Fig. 12) . Initial
steps climb to f 1145 Ma before stepping down to
the final two steps that fall between 1090 and 1097
Ma. These final two steps comprise nearly 50% of the
total age spectrum and are concordant with the age
estimate defined by H98-131.6-2. Despite the com-
plexity of 98GC-25 (presumably caused by excess
argon and/or
39Ar recoil) the best age of this sample is
interpreted to be about 1090 Ma. This interpretation is
Fig. 12. 40Ar/39Ar age spectrum diagrams for biotite from the two mafic sills. The flat spectrum from H98-131.6-2 is interpreted to record
emplacement of the sill at 1090.6 F 4.5 Ma cooling age (2 r error). The final two ca. 1090 Ma steps from the complex spectrum of 98GC-25 are
interpreted to also record cooling at about 1090 Ma.
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220214

### page_17
partially based on the apparent concordance of the
final two heating steps with the simpler spectrum
given by H98-131.6-2.
5. Discussion
The characteristic magnetizations identified in the
Unkar igneous suite and Nankoweap Formation pro-
vide two distinct ancient paleomagnetic pole positions.
The Unkar igneous suite magnetization (UI) is defined
by 16 sites from six different intrusions and three
different flows of the Cardenas Basalts. The directions
for this magnetization are well-defined, of uniform
polarity and are of west-seeking declination and mod-
erate positive inclination. A mean paleomagnetic pole,
calculated assuming a geocentric axial dipole during
the Proterozoic, is located at 32 jN, 185 jE (dp = 6.8,
dm = 9.3) in the north Pacific ( Table 4 ; Fig. 13 ). We
interpret the UI pole to be primary based on a partial
contact test with the host Dox Formation strata.
The Nankoweap Formation magnetization (NA) is
defined by seven sites along a continuous stratigraphic
transect from strata directly overlying the Cardenas
Basalts to immediately below the overlying Tanner
Member of the Chuar Group. The directions for this
magnetization, carried in hematite, are well-defined
and have a west – southwest declination and shallow

### page_18
negative inclination. A mean paleomagnetic pole,
calculated assuming a geocentric axial dipole during
the time of magnetization acquisition, is located at
10jS, 163 jE (dp = 3.5, dm = 7.0) in the south Pacific
(Table 4; Fig. 13). The NA pole is considered primary,
or at least acquired soon after deposition, based on a
positive fold test, and the available field evidence that
suggests that deposition of Nankoweap Formation
strata was synchronous with deformation.
The previous paleomagnetic work done throughout
the Grand Canyon Supergroup, Arizona, represented
an initial attempt to better define the Middle and Late
Proterozoic Laurentia APWP (Elston and Gromme ´,
1974, 1984; Elston and Scott, 1973; Elston, 1986;
Elston, 1989a,b,c) . However, much of this work has
never been published in peer-reviewed journals; some
reports have only been in the form of abstracts (e.g.,
Elston and Gromme´, 1984; Elston, 1986 ), or in the
form of basic compilations of paleomagnetic poles
used in published figures of APWPs. Unfortunately,
both types of publications lack ample presentation of
the raw data, in particular results of progressive
demagnetization, and discussion of any field-based
tests of the antiquity of the magnetizations (e.g.,
Elston, 1989a,b,c ).
Relevant to this study, Elston and Scott (1973)
published paleomagnetic results from Cardenas Basalts
and lowermost strata of the Nankoweap Formation.
They reported three pole positions. These were based
on data from (1) two flows in the Cardenas Basalts,
with a paleopole at 0.4 jN, 174.6jW (10 samples), (2)
five samples from the top weathered-zone of the Car-
denas Basalts, with a paleopole at 49.4 jN, 167.8 jW
and (3) six samples from the lowermost Nankoweap
Formation, with a paleopole at 12.5jN, 174.4jE. None
of the paleomagnetic poles reported by Elston and
Scott (1973) are similar to the results presented in this
study (Table 4). Although there is no obvious reason
for the discrepancy between the two datasets, we offer
some explanations. One is the very small number of
samples and sites collected by Elston and Scott (1973).
Our current analysis revealed that at least one speci-
men, and often several specimens, from every site
within the Unkar igneous suite and the Nankoweap
Formation was characterized by a spurious demagne-
tization response and/or yielded a randomly oriented
magnetization that was not interpretable. Furthermore,
within the Cardenas Basalts only 60% of the flows
gave interpretable demagnetization results. Conse-
quently, the limited sample size of the collection
reported by Elston ad Scott (1973) could have led to
erroneous paleomagnetic directional information and,
thus, inaccurate pole positions. An additional possibil-
ity for the discrepancy is the use of more modern and
sensitive methods and techniques for demagnetization
in the present study compared to those used three
decades ago.
The age of the UI pole is best defined by new
40Ar/39Ar results reported in this study, which provide
an emplacement age of about 1090 Ma for the Unkar
intrusions. Although the dated sills are located outside
the area sampled for the paleomagnetic work, their
age is similar to previously reported isotopic age
determinations for the Cardenas Basalts and associat-
ed intrusions in the study area (Elston and Mckee,
1982; Larson et al., 1994; Timmons et al., 2001) .W e
suggest that the newly dated sills are part of the same
magmatic event that produced the mafic rocks studied
for paleomagnetism and, thus, infer that the UI pole
corresponds to an age of about 1090 Ma. When
plotted on Laurentia’s Proterozoic APWP , the UI pole
is in close agreement with poles derived from other
mafic intrusions, of similar age, from the southwest
US (for review, see Harlan, 1993 ), as well as from

### page_19
Keweenawan rocks of the midcontinent rift system
(Fig. 13) , which have magnetization acquisition ages
of about 1090 – 1100 Ma (for review, see Halls and
Pesonen, 1982 ). We note that whatever process is
responsible for the disturbed 40Ar/39Ar age spectra
reported by Timmons et al. (2001) , which yielded
total gas age estimates ranging from about 988 to 771
Ma, it does not appear to be recorded in the paleo-
magnetism of these rocks. The similarity in age, and
paleomagnetic pole positions, of the Unkar igneous
suite with other mafic suites in the southwest US
(including those that intrude metamorphic rocks of the
Mojave and Arizona terranes, the sedimentary rocks
of the Apache and Pahrump groups and within the
Salt River Canyon), the Pikes Peak Granite batholith
(Smith et al., 1999) and the midcontinent rift system
(van Schmus and Hinze, 1985) indicate pervasive
mafic and related magmatism throughout the Lauren-
tia craton at ca. 1100 Ma (Harlan, 1993) . Heaman et
al. (1992) and Howard (1991) suggest that such a
continent-scale magmatic event may indicate the ini-
tiation of thermal upwelling in the mantle via multiple
plumes. Hoffman (1989) speculated that this large-
scale mantle upwelling was the ultimate consequence
of long-term mantle insulation below a stable super-
continent. Such insulation would result in the upward
deflection of lithosphere geotherms, elevated topog-
raphy, and eventually large-scale melting in the man-
tle. Other possible explanations for such large-scale
magmatism involve extension, either related to initial
stages of continental break-up (Timmons et al., 2001) ,
or to Grenville collision to the east and southeast
(Lambeck, 1983; DeRito et al., 1983) . Although
widespread 1.1 Ga magmatism is well documented
for North America, the driving force(s) and cause(s)
of this event are still elusive and require further study.
The similarity between the UI pole with poles from
the Keweenawan rift system of northeast North Amer-
ica (Fig. 13) also supports the general contention that
there has been only a modest magnitude of rotation of
north-central Arizona (i.e., the Colorado Plateau) with
respect to the stable interior of North America during
the Phanerozoic. We recognize that a comparison
involving a single, reasonably well-dated pole with
the track of poles defined by the Keweenawan rift
system, especially given the orientation of the track
with respect to the plateau, does not allow a robust
estimate of the magnitude of plateau rotation. None-
theless, the overall ensemble of paleomagnetic data
from the GCSG (e.g., Elston, 1989c, 1993; Weil et al.,
1999, Timmons et al., 2001 ; this paper) is coincident
with the Keweenawan Loop and younger, Neoproter-
ozoic results from elsewhere in North America. This
observation contrasts with recent estimates of up to
10 – 15j of clockwise rotation of the plateau based on
paleomagnetic pole comparisons between Upper Tri-
assic strata from the southwest and the east coast of
North America (e.g., Kent and Witte, 1993; Kent and
Olsen, 1997; Steiner and Lucas, 2000 ). For a review
of the Colorado Plateau rotation debate and a rigorous
assessment of the maximum magnitude of plateau
rotation, see Molina Garza et al. (1998) .
The age of the NA pole is less well-defined than
that of the UI pole. No absolute ages have been
reported for the Nankoweap Formation. Previous
age estimates were based on initial paleomagnetic
results (Elston and Scott, 1976; Elston, 1989a,b,c) .
Link et al. (1993) proposed that the lower Nankoweap
member is similar in age to the Cardenas Basalts,
while the upper Nankoweap member would be similar
in age to lower Chuar Group strata. Our new data
from the Nankoweap Formation provide a paleomag-
Fig. 13. Summary apparent polar wander path for Laurentia for the
1100 – 700 Ma time interval. Open circles are selected Keweenawan
and Grenville ‘‘A poles’’ fromWeil et al. (1998) and Warnock et al.
(2000). UI, Cardenas Basalts/intrusions (Unkar Group); NA,
Nankoweap Formation.
A.B. Weil et al. / Tectonophysics 375 (2003) 199–220 217

### page_20
netic pole with an estimated age of f 900 – 850 Ma,
based on its position relative to recently obtained
results from the Chuar Group (Weil et al., 1999) .
The inferred f 200 Ma age difference between the
upper Unkar Group and the Nankoweap Formation
implies that a third major unconformity exists within
the Grand Canyon similar to the estimated magnitudes
of time missing at the Great (Walcott, 1894; Noble,
1914) and Greatest (Noble, 1914) unconformities,
already well-documented. This interpretation is simi-
lar to the proposal of Lucchitta and Hendricks (1983)
that the Nankoweap Formation is considerably youn-
ger than the Cardenas Basalts, and that the unconfor-
mity between the Unkar Group and the Nankoweap
Formation represents a major hiatus in the Grand
Canyon sequence.
6. Conclusions
Paleomagnetic results from the Unkar igneous suite
and Nankoweap Formation, GCSG, Arizona yield two
primary paleomagnetic poles for Laurentia for the latest
Middle and early Late Proterozoic (Fig. 13) .N e w
40Ar/39Ar age determinations from an Unkar sill give
an interpreted intrusion age of about 1090 Ma, similar
to previously reported geochronologic data for the
Cardenas Basalts and associated intrusions (Fig. 12) .
The pole position for the Unkar Group Cardenas
Basalts and intrusions is in good agreement with ca.
1100 Ma paleomagnetic poles from the Keweenawan
midcontinent rift deposits ( Halls and Pesonen, 1982;
Harlan, 1993 and references therein) and other SW
Laurentia diabase bodies ( Harlan, 1993 and references
therein). The close agreement in age and position of the
UI pole with poles derived from rift related rocks from
the southwest and Keweenawan of Laurentia indicate
that mafic magmatism was essentially synchronous and
wide spread throughout Laurentia at ca. 1100 Ma,
suggesting a large-scale continental mafic magmatic
event (Howard, 1991) . The pole position for the Nan-
koweap Formation, 40 j south of that from the Unkar
mafic rocks, argues for a considerably younger age of
deposition, about 900 Ma, than has previously been
proposed. Consequently, the f 200 Ma difference in
age between the Cardenas Basalts and overlying Nan-
koweap Formation provides evidence for a third major
unconformity within the Grand Canyon sequence.
Acknowledgements
Chris Powell was an enthusiastic, inspiring and
prolific academician. His career work on Gondwana-
land and Rodinia has paved the way for many new
ideas and exciting research. He will be dearly missed
as a colleague, scientist and friend. The following
individuals assisted us in sampling in the Grand
Canyon: Carol M. Dehler, Karl E. Karlstrom, J.
Michael Timmons and Susannah Porter. We also
thank the Grand Canyon National Park for our
research agreement and sampling permit. This study
was supported by the National Science Foundation,
Division of Earth Sciences, grant EAR-9706541 (to
Karlstrom, Geissman and Elrick), and a University of
Michigan Scott Turner Fund grant awarded to A.
Weil. Some of this research was made possible by a
Visiting Fellowship at the Institute for Rock Magnet-
ism (IRM) at the University of Minnesota. The IRM is
funded by the Instruments and Facilities Program,
Earth Sciences Division, National Science Founda-
tion, and by the W.M. Keck Foundation. We would
like to thank Stephen Harlan, Bob Butler and Randy
Enkin for their helpful comments, which greatly
improved the quality of this paper.
